newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SA WEEK AHEAD-M3, CREDIT REACTION IMMEDIATE FOCUS.
newsitem.headline: SA WEEK AHEAD-M3, CREDIT REACTION IMMEDIATE FOCUS.

text.p: Last Friday's money supply and bank credit extension figures will be the main immediate domestic focus for South African markets in a three-day holiday-shortened week.
South African money supply ballooned in March but private bank credit extension growth was lower than expected, relieving markets' worst fears over Friday's keenly-awaited data.
Hawkish comments from Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals had triggered fears of a worse-than-expected credit figure.
In fact, preliminary annual private sector credit growth was 15.96 percent, less than the Reuters market consensus of 16.50 percent.
"The important number is credit and that is coming down, which is very nice...Stals obviously didn't know the credit figure when he made his speech," said Dawie Roodt of stockbroker Equisec.
Nick Barnardt of BOE NatWest agreed the unadjusted 3.68 billion rand rise in private bank credit last month was moderate but said the surge in broadly defined M3 money supply was alarming.
M3 grew 16.39 percent year-on-year in March, way above the market consensus for a 15.04 percent rise.
"Overall the data is probably neutral for interest rates but the huge jump in M3 is worrying," Barnardt said, noting that this figure had increased 9.02 billion in the month.
In the last two months M3 had expanded by 17.27 billion rand, or over five percent, he added.

One bond dealer said the data put a bit of a question-mark around Stals' remarks at a conference in Durban on Friday morning when he cautioned monetary policy might have to be tightened further to curb liquidity and excessive credit growth.
Roodt said the central bank governor appeared to be following in Federal Reserve chairman's Alan Greenspan's footsteps in trying to deflate any "irrational exuberance" in the market.
"I think his comments should be seen as caution to the market more than anything else," he said.
The only major indicator due this week is headline gold and foreign reserves, at 1600 GMT on Friday.
Economists said offshore demand for bonds and shares should lift the figure but it was too early to make detailed forecasts for the month-end.
Some increase in the underlying reserves position has been discounted after healthy portfolio investment in South Africa this month which has held the rand steady.
